source_text: Προφανεῖς μὲν οὖν καὶ πᾶσαι αἱ ἄλλαι ἀρεταί, αἱ παρὰ τῷ Μωυσεῖ ἀναγεγραμμέναι, ἀρχὴν Ἕλλησι παντὸς τοῦ ἠθικοῦ τόπου παρασχόμεναι, ἀνδρείαν λέγω καὶ σωφροσύνην καὶ φρόνησιν καὶ δικαιοσύνην καρτερίαν τε καὶ ὑπομονὴν καὶ τὴν σεμνότητα καὶ ἐγκράτειαν τήν τε ἐπὶ τούτοις εὐσέβειαν. ἀλλ’ ἡ μὲν εὐσέβεια παντί που δήλη τὸ ἀνωτάτω καὶ πρεσβύτατον αἴτιον σέβειν καὶ τιμᾶν καὶ διδάσκουσα. καὶ δικαιοσύνην δὲ αὐτὸς ὁ νόμος παρίστησι παιδεύων τήν τε φρόνησιν διὰ τῆς τῶν αἰσθητῶν εἰδώλων ἀποχῆς καὶ τῆς πρὸς τὸν ποιητὴν καὶ πατέρα τῶν ὅλων προσκληρώσεως, ἀφ’ ἧς δόξης οἷον πηγῆς πᾶσα σύνεσις αὔξεται. θυσίαι γὰρ ἀνόμων βδέλυγμα κυρίῳ, εὐχαὶ δὲ κατευθυνόντων δεκταὶ παρ’ αὐτῷ. ἐπεὶ οιαῦτα καὶ τὰ παρὰ Ἡσαΐᾳ· τί μοι πλῆθος τῶν θυσιῶν ὑμῶν ὑμῶν; λέγει κύριος, καὶ πᾶσα ἡ περικοπή· λῦε πάντα σύνδεσμον ἀδικίας· αὕτη γὰρ θυσία θεῷ δεκτή, καρδία συντετριμμένη καὶ ζητοῦσα τὸν πεπλακότα. ζυγὰ δόλια βδέλυγμα ἔναντι θεοῦ, στάθμιον δὲ δίκαιον δεκτὸν αὐτῷ. ἐντεῦθεν ζυγὸν μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν Πυθαγόρας παραινεῖ. δικαιοσύνη δὲ δολία εἴρηται ἡ τῶν αἱρέσεων ἐπαγγελία, καὶ γλῶσσα μὲν ἀδίκων ἐξολεῖται, στόμα δὲ δικαίων ἀποστάζει σοφίαν. ἀλλὰ γὰρ τοὺς σοφοὺς καὶ φρονίμους φαύλους καλοῦσιν. μακρὸν δ’ ἂν εἴη περὶ τῶν ἀρετῶν τούτων μαρτυρίας παρατίθεσθαι, ἁπάσης ταύτας ἐξυμνούσης τῆς γραφῆς. ἐπεὶ δ’ οὖν τὴν μὲν ἀνδρείαν ὁρίζονται ἐπιστήμην δεινῶν καὶ οὐ δεινῶν καὶ τῶν μεταξύ, τὴν δὲ σωφροσύνην ἕξιν ἐν αἱρέσει καὶ φυγῇ σῴζουσαν τὰ τῆς φρονήσεως κρίματα, παράκειται τε τῇ μὲν ἀνδρείᾳ ἥ τε ὑπομονή, ἣν καρτερίαν καλοῦσιν, ἐπιστήμην ἐμμενετέων καὶ οὐκ ἐμμενετέων, ἥ τε μεγαλοψυχία, ἐπιστήμη τῶν συμβαινόντων ὑπεραίρουσα, ἀλλὰ καὶ τῇ σωφροσύνῃ ἡ εὐλάβεια, ἔκκλισις οὖσα σὺν λόγῳ. Φυλακὴ δὲ τῶν ἐντολῶν, τήρησις οὖσα αὐτῶν ἀβλαβής, περιποίησίς ἐστιν ἀσφαλείας βίου. καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν ἄνευ ἀνδρείας καρτερικὸν εἶναι οὐδὲ μὴν ἄνευ σωφροσύνης ἐγκρατῆ. ἀντακολουθοῦσι δὲ ἀλλήλαις αἱ ἀρεταί, καἰ παρ’ ᾧ αἱ τῶν ἀρετῶν ἀκολουθίαι, παρὰ τούτῳ καὶ ἡ σωτηρία, τήρησις οὖσα τοῦ εὖ ἔχοντος. εἰκότως ἔτι περὶ τούτων διαλαβόντες τῶν ἀρετῶν περὶ πασῶν ἂν εἴημεν ἐσκεμμένοι, ὅτι ὁ μίαν ἔχων ἀρετὴν γνωστικῶς πάσας ἔχει διὰ τὴν ἀντακολουθίαν. αὐτίκα ἡ ἐγκράτεια διάθεσίς ἐστιν ἀνυπέρβατος τῶν κατὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον φανέντων. ἐγκρατεύεται δὲ ὁ κατέχων τὰς παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον ὁρμὰς ἢ ὁ κατέχων αὑτὸν ὥστε μὴ ὁρμᾶν παρὰ τὸν ὀρθὸν λόγον. σωφροσύνη δὲ αὕτη οὐκ ἄνευ ἀνδρείας, ἐπειδὴ ἐξ ἐντολῶν γίνεται ἑπομένη τῷ διατεταγμένῳ θεῷ φρόνησίς τε καὶ ἡ μιμητικὴ τῆς θείας διαθέσεως δικαιοσύνη, καθ’ ἣν ἐγκρατευόμενοι καθαροὶ πρὸς εὐσέβειαν καὶ τὴν ἑπομένην ἀκολούθως τῷ θεῷ πρᾶξιν στελλόμεθα, ἐξομοιούμενοι τῷ κυρίῳ κατὰ τὸ δυνατὸν ἡμῖν, ἐπικήροις τὴν φύσιν ὑπάρχουσιν.
thought_title: Virtues in Greek and Christian Thought
pass_a_gloss: Virtues are therefore obvious, and all the other virtues recorded by Moses provide a starting point for the Greeks for all ethical matters, I mean courage and self-control and prudence and justice and patience and perseverance and dignity and self-control and the piety that is based on these. But piety is somehow evident to everyone as the highest and oldest cause to reverence and honor and teach. And the law itself also presents justice, teaching prudence through the avoidance of sensory idols and the calling towards the creator and father of all, from which glory, as if from a source, all understanding increases. For sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but prayers of the upright are acceptable to him. Since also the things from Isaiah say: what is the multitude of your sacrifices to me, says the Lord, and the whole passage says: loose every bond of injustice, for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a heart broken and seeking the one who has been afflicted. Deceptive scales are an abomination before God, but a just balance is acceptable to him. From this, Pythagoras advises not to exceed the balance. But justice is said to be deceptive, the promise of the sects, and the tongue of the unrighteous will be destroyed, but the mouth of the righteous will drip with wisdom. And yet they call the wise and prudent ones worthless. It would be long to set forth testimonies about these virtues, which all of scripture praises. Since, therefore, they define courage as knowledge of things to be feared and not to be feared and of the things in between, and self-control as a state that saves the judgments of prudence in choice and avoidance, perseverance, which they call patience, is set beside courage, knowledge of things to be endured and not to be endured, and magnanimity, knowledge of things that happen, surpassing them, but also caution is set beside self-control, being a withdrawal with reason. The guarding of the commandments, being a blameless keeping of them, is a preservation of a secure life. And it is not possible to be patient without courage or self-controlled without self-control. The virtues follow one another, and where the sequences of the virtues are, there also is salvation, being a keeping of what is well-ordered. It is likely that, having taken up these virtues, we would be concerned with all of them, because the one who has one virtue knowingly has all of them through their mutual following. Immediately, self-control is a disposition that is unconquerable regarding the things that appear according to the right reason. And one is self-controlled who holds back the impulses that are contrary to the right reason or who holds himself back so as not to be impelled contrary to the right reason. But self-control is not without courage, since it comes from the commandments, following the God who has been ordained, and prudence and the justice that imitates the divine disposition, according to which, being self-controlled, we are pure towards piety and the action that follows God, being conformed to the Lord as much as possible, having a nature that is subordinate.

pass_b_english: All the virtues recorded by Moses are therefore evident, and they gave the Greeks a starting point for every aspect of ethics: I mean courage, self-control, prudence, justice, patience, perseverance, dignity, self-control, and the piety that rests on these. Piety is somehow clear to everyone as the highest and most ancient cause to revere, honor, and teach. The law itself also sets forth justice, instructing prudence through the avoidance of sensory idols and the calling toward the Creator and Father of all, from whose glory, as from a source, all understanding grows. For the sacrifices of the lawless are an abomination to the Lord, but the prayers of the upright are acceptable to him (Isaiah 1:11). And Isaiah says the same: 'What is the multitude of your sacrifices to me?' says the Lord, and the whole passage declares: 'Loose every bond of injustice,' for this is a sacrifice acceptable to God, a broken heart seeking the one who fashioned it (Isaiah 58:6). Deceptive scales are an abomination before God, but a just balance is acceptable to him. From this, Pythagoras advises not to exceed the balance. Yet justice is called deceptive — the promise of the sects — and the tongue of the unrighteous will be destroyed, but the mouth of the righteous drips with wisdom. And yet they call the wise and prudent worthless. It would take too long to lay out testimonies about these virtues, which all Scripture praises.

Since they define courage as knowledge of things to be feared, things not to be feared, and the things in between, and self-control as a state that preserves the judgments of prudence in choice and avoidance, perseverance — which they call patience — stands beside courage as knowledge of what must be endured and what must not, and magnanimity stands beside it as knowledge of events that surpasses them. Caution also stands beside self-control as a withdrawal guided by reason. Keeping the commandments, which is a blameless observance of them, is the preservation of a secure life. One cannot be patient without courage, nor self-controlled without self-control. The virtues follow one another, and where the sequences of the virtues are, there also is salvation, which is the keeping of what is well-ordered. It is fitting, then, that by taking up these virtues we would be versed in all of them, because the one who knowingly possesses one virtue possesses them all through their mutual sequence.

Self-control is a disposition unconquerable by the impulses that appear according to right reason. A person is self-controlled who restrains impulses contrary to right reason, or who restrains himself so as not to be driven contrary to right reason. But self-control does not exist without courage, since it arises from the commandments, following the God-ordained prudence and the justice that imitates the divine disposition. In accordance with this, as we exercise self-control we become pure toward piety and the action that follows God, conforming ourselves to the Lord as far as we can, having a nature that is subordinate.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal rendering, while Pass B provides a more fluent version with necessary scripture citations (Isaiah 1:11 and Isaiah 58:6) which were alluded to in the Greek. The translation of 'ἐπικήροις τὴν φύσιν ὑπάρχουσιν' as 'having a nature that is subordinate' (Pass A) and 'having a nature that is subordinate' (Pass B) correctly handles the Greek term.
